cells.tense: Present — here, holding what's yours and setting down what isn't.
cells.verb: carrying what's yours and setting down what's finished, with a steady hand on both
cells.place: where you pick a direction and mean it
cells.ask: Tend one small thing — not to drive it, just to see what it does when you look after it; the way you let go of what's done can start feeding what's still growing.
cells.core:
You're pointing somewhere, and you're not dragging everything behind you to get there. What's finished you've set down; what's yours you carry without complaint. That's why the choosing feels clean right now — the hand holding the direction isn't also clutching the last one.

There's room in that for something you haven't needed yet: looking after a thing just to watch it come along, without steering it. Pick something small and tend it, and let it keep its own pace. The same ease you have with endings can learn to sit with beginnings.
cells.sheetLine: You carry what's yours and set down what's done, and the direction stays clear.

cells.tense: Future — already deciding how this ends before it's there.
cells.verb: calling things finished ahead of time and cutting them loose
cells.place: where you pick a direction and mean it
cells.ask: Before you let the next thing go, look at it plainly and ask what's actually in front of you — not what you've decided is coming. When the letting go waits for the thing to be done, it starts to feel like finishing instead of losing.
cells.core:
You're letting go of things before they've asked to be let go of. Somewhere ahead there's a version where this costs you, and you're already paying for it — setting things down early, cutting loose what hasn't finished, so you won't be caught holding it when the ending comes. It looks like decisiveness. It's bracing.

The release is running on a forecast, not on the thing itself. Slow the hand enough to check: is this done, or do I just want it over? One honest look at what's actually here, before you cut, will tell you which.
cells.sheetLine: You're letting go before anything's finished, to beat the ending to it.

cells.tense: Past — still standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.verb: holding on past the point where holding did any good
cells.place: where you pick a direction and mean it
cells.ask: Don't push yourself to let go. Put your hands on something you can build and make solid — one thing that will still be standing next month. When there's something that holds, what's done tends to fall away on its own.
cells.core:
Something ended, and you haven't set it down. The direction you'd pick next is right there, but your hands are still full of the last one — so you're not quite choosing, you're waiting, and the waiting looks like loyalty. It isn't disloyal to put down what's finished.

The thing to do isn't to force the letting go; that just makes the grip tighter. It's to build something. One steady piece of work, something that holds weight and stays. Let the grip loosen while your hands are busy with what's actually yours now. You'll know it's done when setting the old thing down feels like finishing it, not like giving up.
cells.sheetLine: You're still carrying what ended, so you can't quite choose what's next.

cells.tense: Present, disowned — the choosing is yours and you're calling it circumstance.
cells.verb: deciding what to keep carrying and what to drop, every day, by what you do
cells.place: where you pick a direction and mean it
cells.ask: Pick one small thing and look after it on purpose — tend it, and say out loud that you chose to. When the choosing has your name on it, letting the rest go stops feeling like something that happened to you.
cells.core:
You're already steering. What you've let fall away, what you keep showing up for, what you've quietly stopped feeding — that's a set of choices, and you're the one making them. But you talk about it as if it just went that way. The hand is on the direction; the voice says there isn't one.

Start smaller than the big decisions you'd rather not own. Take one thing that's yours to look after and tend it deliberately, and name it as yours. Once you've said "I chose this" about something small, the larger letting-go starts looking like what it is: you, finishing things.
cells.sheetLine: You're already choosing what to carry and what to drop. You call it how things went.
